items.title: Jerome Richardson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, March 9, 1996
items.q: The only one I know of that really did something and has made his mark is Clark Terry. ... I can talk about how great Clark Terry is for years and years, you know, and how wonderful he is.

ctx.x: It’s nice that he has a big band to play in too, because there’s not all the opportunities I guess that there used to be as far as —

Well there are good things to say about big bands and good things to say about small groups. In a small group you have a chance to play on every piece. In a big band, there is no way that everybody can play on a piece, you know, so sometimes there’s one guy, sometimes it’s another and this and that. There are times when you really don’t get a chance to play what you feel in a big band. You don’t have time to play it. Somebody else is doing it. And in that you’re better off in a way playing with a small group,…
Most of them came back to the band, didn’t they?

items.title: Terry Clark — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Jerome Richardson. They all came in a band collectively from California. They were recruited like we were in St. Louis...

ctx.x: Marshal Royal, Ernie Royal. I don’t know whether – is Jerome Richardson from there?

Jerome Richardson. They all came in a band collectively from California. They were recruited like we were in St. Louis, but we were already ensconced there. We had the upper hand. They came in as a bunch of recruits. I think it might have been pre­ arranged, but they were to have been trained at Great Lakes and formed into a band and sent back to some base in – I think it was Treasure Island in California.
Gerald Wilson was part of that?
